solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Hindrance in hotel — cats bouncing around

indicators.note: around tells us the concealed run must be turned the other way to read correctly
in tells us the letters sit inside the run of words that follows, crossing the word breaks

explanation.surface: A hotel's resident cats charging about are getting in everyone's way.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' points to the letters OTEL CATS BO inside 'hotel — cats bouncing', and 'around' turns them back to front. 'Bouncing' looks like an anagram signal but only supplies its first two letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A hindrance is an obstruction or barrier standing in one's way, the plain synonym.

clue.text: Type in dark black showing impudence?

definitions.meaning: printing type with heavy dark strokes, used for emphasis
a brazen, cheeky manner; the ... person shows nerve, hence the question mark

explanation.walkthrough: The second sense stretches things a little: the adjective for cheeky is usually bold-faced, which the question mark acknowledges.
explanation.definitionFit: Heavy printing type is called by this name, and a brazen face shows cheek or nerve.

clue.text: A sot getting drunk with extraordinary smart set? They will raise a glass

indicators.note: a sot getting drunk is reeling about, so these three words' letters are thrown into disorder

parts.note: taken as written for the first anagram

indicators.note: extraordinary means out of its usual form, so the following two words are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written for the second anagram

explanation.surface: A drunkard joins high society at a party, and they all lift their glasses.
explanation.walkthrough: Two anagrams side by side: 'getting drunk' turns A SOT into TOAS, and 'extraordinary' turns SMART SET into TMASTERS.
explanation.definitionFit: These masters of ceremonies propose the toasts at formal dinners, so they lead everyone in raising glasses.

clue.text: About to get present in box

parts.note: C is short for circa, Latin for about, used with dates
to present something is to offer it

explanation.surface: Someone is about to receive a gift packed in a box.
explanation.definitionFit: A coffer is a strongbox or chest for keeping money and valuables.

clue.text: Fellow conveyed by the rickshaw

indicators.note: conveyed by says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: A man is being carried along in a rickshaw.
explanation.definitionFit: Crosswords use any man's first name for a fellow, a generic male person.

clue.text: Person not recognised in street, park officer

parts.note: a ranger patrols and looks after a park or forest

explanation.surface: A park warden spots an unfamiliar face out in the street.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone you do not know or recognise is an unknown, unfamiliar person to you.

clue.text: Anxiety and fright when son has bunked off

indicators.note: to bunk off is to skip school, so the son's letter goes missing from the word

parts.note: a fright is a scare
S is the abbreviation for son in genealogies

explanation.surface: A parent's worry and alarm when a boy has played truant from school.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bunk off' is British slang for playing truant.
explanation.definitionFit: Care in the sense of worry or concern, as in 'without a care in the world'.

clue.text: See delta possibly from valley

indicators.note: possibly suggests one possible arrangement of these letters among many

parts.note: taken as written for the anagram

explanation.surface: Look at the river mouth, perhaps, from down in the valley.
explanation.walkthrough: 'See' looks like a bishop's diocese, but it is simply anagram fodder. The answer is a valley in the north of England, of the River Tees.
explanation.definitionFit: The dale of the River Tees is a named valley in northern England; dale means valley.

clue.text: Poison making ten Arabs ill

indicators.note: ill means unwell or out of sorts, so these letters are disordered

parts.note: taken as written for the anagram

explanation.surface: A toxin is making ten Arab men sick.
explanation.definitionFit: This old name for rat poison, usually arsenic, is literally the bane of rats.

clue.text: Request quiet, wanting heavy metal curtailed

parts.note: P is piano, the musical direction for quiet

indicators.note: curtailed means having its tail cut off, so the final letter goes

parts.note: lead is a famously heavy metal

explanation.surface: Someone asks for some peace, not wanting loud heavy metal music cut short.
explanation.walkthrough: 'curtailed' removes the last letter of LEAD, giving LEA.
explanation.definitionFit: A plea is an earnest request or appeal for something.

clue.text: Burglars? They pose no danger at Christmas!

definitions.text: They pose no danger at Christmas!
definitions.meaning: festive crackers that are harmless when pulled, read as two words

explanation.walkthrough: Split into two words, the answer is harmless party crackers pulled at Christmas dinner, a British tradition with paper hats and jokes inside.
explanation.definitionFit: Thieves who break into strongboxes are called this, and harmless festive bangers fit the split reading.

clue.text: Rehearsed orchestral players will appreciate the situation

definitions.meaning: after rehearsal the musicians are familiar with the written music in front of them
to understand what is going on, an idiom

explanation.walkthrough: Literally, the orchestra has learned its sheet music; idiomatically, someone grasps the facts of a situation.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means to be aware of the facts, and literally describes musicians familiar with their written music.

clue.text: Fragrance said to be evident in castle

parts.note: balm can mean a sweet scent or fragrance
oral means spoken or said rather than written

explanation.surface: A sweet perfume is said to hang about a stately castle.
explanation.walkthrough: BALMORAL is the British royal family's castle in the Scottish Highlands.
explanation.definitionFit: Balmoral is a royal castle in Aberdeenshire, the monarch's Scottish summer residence.

clue.text: Fish, angler's first to be caught in lake

indicators.note: to be caught in a place is to be held inside it, so one piece goes inside the other

parts.note: loch is the Scottish word for a lake

indicators.note: first takes just the opening letter of the angler's word

explanation.surface: A fisherman's first catch in the lake is a fish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'angler's first' is A, which goes inside LOCH.
explanation.definitionFit: A loach is a small freshwater fish with whisker-like barbels around its mouth.

clue.text: A girl excited about love — one's often sung in church

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so one piece wraps round the other
excited means stirred up, so these letters are agitated into a new order

parts.note: taken as written for the anagram
love is nil in tennis, which looks like the letter O

explanation.surface: An excited girl is thinking about her love.
explanation.walkthrough: 'excited' rearranges A GIRL to GLRIA, and 'about' puts it round O.
explanation.definitionFit: The Gloria is a hymn of praise, part of the Mass, regularly sung at church services.

clue.text: Extremely stupid neglecting English studies

indicators.note: neglecting means leaving out, so the letter for English is dropped

parts.note: dense means very slow-witted or stupid

explanation.surface: Someone thoroughly dim is skipping English lessons.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Extremely' looks like a call to take the outer letters of 'stupid', but it is part of the definition of DENSE.
explanation.definitionFit: A den is a private study or snug room where one works, so dens are studies.

clue.text: No longer with us, having relaxed after end of year

indicators.note: after puts the relaxed piece behind the end of year piece

parts.note: December is the last month, abbreviated DEC
eased means loosened or relaxed

explanation.surface: Someone has wound down after the year closed, and is gone.
explanation.definitionFit: Deceased means dead, which is the polite meaning of no longer with us.

clue.text: Natural ability — it's something flashy, they say

indicators.note: they say means as people pronounce it, so we want a word sounding like another

parts.note: a flare is a bright flash of light, as from a signal rocket

explanation.surface: Someone's innate talent is said to be rather showy.
explanation.definitionFit: Flair is an instinctive aptitude or talent for doing something well.

clue.text: Bird trainer once working between one river and another

indicators.note: between puts the reworked letters into the gap separating the two rivers

parts.note: the Fal is a river in Cornwall
R is the abbreviation for river

indicators.note: working means in operation or being worked over, so these letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written for the anagram

explanation.surface: A man who used to train birds is now busy between two rivers.
explanation.walkthrough: The Fal is a river in Cornwall, England; 'once working' looks like 'formerly employed' in the surface but is an anagram.
explanation.definitionFit: A falconer trains hawks and falcons to hunt, so is a trainer of birds.

clue.text: Record wild animal at edge of forest

indicators.note: edge of here means the leading letter of the word

parts.note: an ape is a wild animal

explanation.surface: Someone films a wild beast at the fringe of the woods.
explanation.definitionFit: To tape something is to record it on magnetic tape.

clue.text: In favour of money to set forth as a reward

parts.note: pro means for or in favour of
the pound is British money

explanation.surface: Someone is all for putting cash up as a prize.
explanation.walkthrough: To propound is usually to put forward an idea, but an older sense is to offer something as a prize.
explanation.definitionFit: An old sense of propound is to offer up or hold out a prize, as for a competition.

clue.text: Food in a series of instalments as you might say?

indicators.note: as you might say means as it is pronounced, so one word sounds like another

parts.note: a serial is a story told in a series of instalments

explanation.surface: Food that arrives in parts, as it were.
explanation.definitionFit: Cereal is a grain food, typically eaten at breakfast.

clue.text: The male would get bigger, full of energy — one growing up in the country?

definitions.text: one growing up in the country

parts.note: he'd is short for he would

indicators.note: full of means containing, so one piece holds the other

parts.note: to grow is to get bigger
E is the physics symbol for energy

explanation.surface: A man would grow, full of energy, as a country lad growing up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'full of' puts E inside GROW, giving GEROW.
explanation.definitionFit: A hedgerow is a row of bushes and trees growing alongside a country field or lane.

clue.text: Hate journalist turning up to face trial

indicators.note: turning up in a down clue means read from bottom to top, so the letters go backwards

parts.note: ED is short for editor, a journalist
a test is a trial

explanation.surface: A reporter hates appearing in court to face a trial.
explanation.walkthrough: 'turning up' reverses ED, giving DE.
explanation.definitionFit: To detest is to hate or loathe intensely.

clue.text: Satiric actor turning 'blue'

indicators.note: turning means changing form, so these letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written for the anagram

explanation.surface: A satirical comedian starts telling dirty jokes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'blue' looks like meaning smutty, the actor's turn, but here it is blue-blooded, noble.
explanation.definitionFit: Blue blood is noble birth, so blue in quotes means of high, noble rank.

clue.text: Confectionery from van is offered outside church?

indicators.note: offered outside means placed round the outside, so one piece wraps the other

parts.note: CE stands for the Church of England

explanation.surface: Sweets from a van are on sale outside a church.
explanation.walkthrough: The van is an ice-cream van, the kind that tours British streets playing chimes; the question mark admits church is only an abbreviation here.
explanation.definitionFit: Ices are frozen treats such as ice creams, sold from vans.

clue.text: Part of sail that could spell danger to sailor

definitions.meaning: a section of sail that can be rolled up to reduce its area
a ridge of rock or coral just under the sea, a hazard to ships

explanation.definitionFit: A reef is a section of sail that can be taken in, and also a ridge of rocks hazardous to ships.

clue.text: Something burdensome, like the round of drinks we buy

definitions.meaning: a responsibility or obligation that weighs on someone

definitions.text: like the round of drinks we buy
definitions.meaning: a round we pay for is our treat, read as two words

explanation.walkthrough: Read as two words, the answer is what you say when your group pays for the round.
explanation.definitionFit: An onus is a burden or duty, and read as two words it says we are paying.

clue.text: Something the scientific observer gets close to?

definitions.text: Something the scientific observer gets close to?

parts.words: Something the scientific observer gets close to?
parts.note: the observer is read as the scientist's seeing organ, pressed up to the lens of a microscope

explanation.walkthrough: 'observer' suggests a person, but it is the scientist's eye, placed close to the lens of a microscope.
explanation.definitionFit: The lens nearest the eye in a microscope or telescope is the one you look into.

clue.text: Big leaders, idiots

definitions.meaning: large heads, a leader being a head, read as two words

explanation.definitionFit: Fatheads are dim people, and split up the word gives large heads, heads being leaders.
